## Learning outcomes

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- explain the difference between a Quarto source file and its rendered output;
- recognize the main parts of a Quarto document;
- add headings, text, lists, and inline code;
- add and run a simple R code chunk; and
- render a `.qmd` file to HTML.

## 1. What is Quarto?

Quarto lets you combine:

- written explanations;
- formatted text;
- R code;
- code output;
- tables; and
- figures

in one reproducible document.

A Quarto source file ends in:

```text
.qmd
```

When you render the file, Quarto creates a finished document such as:

```text
.html
```

::: {.callout-important}
Edit the `.qmd` file, not the rendered `.html` file.
:::

## 2. Examine the YAML header

The information at the top of this document is called the **YAML header**:

```yaml
---
title: "Introduction to Quarto"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    embed-resources: true
editor: source
---
```

The YAML header controls how the document is rendered.

- `title` sets the document title.
- `format: html` creates an HTML document.
- `toc: true` adds a table of contents.
- `embed-resources: true` puts supporting files inside the HTML file.
- `editor: source` opens the document in source mode.

::: {.callout-note}
The opening and closing `---` lines belong only around the YAML header at the top of the document.
:::

## 3. Add formatted text

Quarto uses Markdown syntax for text formatting.

Type the following below this section:

```markdown
### About me

My name is **Your Name**.

I am interested in *your research interest*.

One thing I want to learn in this course is `your answer`.
```

Replace the placeholder text with your own information.

### Common Markdown syntax

| What you want | What you type |
|---|---|
| Heading | `## Heading` |
| Bold text | `**bold text**` |
| Italic text | `*italic text*` |
| Inline code | `` `read_csv()` `` |
| Bullet | `- item` |
| Numbered item | `1. item` |
| Link | `[Quarto](https://quarto.org)` |

## 4. Add a list

Add a heading and a short list:

```markdown
### Files in my course project

- `course-hub/`
- `tutorials-exercises/`
- `homework-repos/`
```

A trailing `/`, such as in `course-hub/`, indicates a folder.

## 5. Add an R code chunk

A code chunk lets you include executable R code inside a Quarto document.

Insert a new R code chunk using:

- **Mac:** `Option + Command + I`
- **Windows:** `Ctrl + Alt + I`

Then enter:

```{r}
message <- "Hello, Quarto!"
message
```

Click the green triangle in the upper-right corner of the chunk to run it.

You should see:

```text
[1] "Hello, Quarto!"
```

::: {.callout-note}
You do not need to understand every part of this R code yet. The goal is to see how code and output can appear together in one document.
:::

## 6. Render the document

To create the finished HTML document:

1. Save the `.qmd` file.
2. Click **Render** at the top of the Source pane.
3. Wait for Quarto to finish.
4. View the rendered HTML document.

Rendering checks the document from top to bottom and creates:

```text
tutorial-01-quarto.html
```

Quarto creates a separate `_files/` folder that contains required CSS, JavaScript, images, and other dependencies. Don't worry about this folder - you don't need to touch it or move it.

## 7. Make one change and render again

Return to the `.qmd` file and add:

```markdown
### One thing I learned

Write one sentence about Quarto here.
```

Then:

1. Save the file.
2. Render it again.
3. Confirm that the new section appears in the HTML output.

## 8. Save your work with Git

In the Git pane:

1. Review the changed `.qmd` and `.html` files.
2. Check the boxes beside the files you want to commit.
3. Click **Commit**.
4. Use a message such as:

```text
complete Quarto tutorial
```

5. Click **Push**.

## Completion checklist

- [ ] I know that `.qmd` is the editable source file.
- [ ] I know that `.html` is the rendered output.
- [ ] I added formatted text using Markdown.
- [ ] I added and ran an R code chunk.
- [ ] I rendered the document successfully.
- [ ] I committed and pushed my work.

## One-sentence summary

> Quarto combines text, code, output, and figures in one reproducible document.
